audio_caption: The audio clip features one male speaker explaining Newton's theory of light, describing how Newton proposed light is made up of particles, using the example of a bulb and imagining "bullets coming out" as particles called "corpuscles." The speaker maintains an informative and slightly academic tone throughout.

The audio clip starts with a single male speaker discussing a Dutch physicist. He stumbles on the pronunciation of the physicist's name, correcting himself and commenting on how it is properly said before deciding to continue using his initial pronunciation.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker discussing the wave nature of light, comparing it to water waves and questioning what particles are vibrating in light. The speaker conveys this with a neutral, informative tone.

The clip features a single male speaker with an informative tone. He mentions "Huygens", discussing "particles everywhere" in the universe, and introduces "ether medium", which he notes was a popular idea at the time. He notes that this medium was everywhere, "sort of like air", and "light" is carried by the vibrations of this medium.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing the visualization of light propagation through an ether medium. He uses an animated example with a lightbulb, explaining that "these particles are the particles of the ether medium," imagining light as "disturbance propagated by the vibrations of the ether particle," or "ripples in the ether medium." His tone is enthusiastic and descriptive.

A single male speaker begins by discussing the difference between the ripples of light and the ripples of water, explaining that water waves are on the surface, which is two-dimensional, and that these ripples are circular. His tone is informative.

The audio begins with a male speaker describing light as a wave in three dimensions and how the ripples are spherical. The speaker emphasizes this as a major difference. Next, the speaker poses the question of what these ripples exactly are, whether it's light or water, and then states, "let me get rid of this and talk about that."

A male speaker begins by asking "So, what exactly are these ripples?" before explaining their scientific name, "wavefronts." His tone is explanatory, preparing to clarify the concept. He mentions they will encounter the word frequently in future videos, reassuring the listener. He continues, stating he will define wavefronts first, and then show them, indicating a visual aid may follow.

The audio features a single male speaker, who is explaining a concept with a calm and educational tone, describing how "wavefronts are basically a set of particles... vibrating in sync with each other, we call them in phase with each other." The speaker seems to be explaining something technical, using terms like "ripples" and "wavefronts."

A male speaker, in a calm, explanatory tone, notes that "the same would be true for our light as well" and brings back a visualization. He then elaborates, "if I were to concentrate on one of those spheres... what you are finding now is, look, all the particles... are vibrating in sync with each other." He then repeats to confirm this point, and concludes by defining those synchronized particles as "wavefronts." He concludes with the question, "what, in general, would be the shape of these wavefronts?"

The audio clip starts with a male speaker explaining a concept using the example of water disturbance. He uses a conversational and explanatory tone, describing ripples forming circular wavefronts if disturbed at one point. He transitions to discussing what happens when disturbed all around, leading to messed up wavefronts with weird shapes. He then states the same principle applies to light as well. The clip concludes with him mentioning looking at an animation.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker discussing light sources and wave fronts, explaining how tiny light sources or distance create spherical wave fronts, contrasting it with closer proximity to larger light sources altering this shape. He pauses to ask the listener to consider the wave front shape at a great distance. He suggests the listener to pause the video and think. After which he says all right.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing how "a sphere would appear flat to us." He gives an example of Earth looking flat and says he will show us how. He mentions being "really far away" from the sphere he is talking about and explains that what we're seeing is actually "flat surfaces." He then mentions that "we are getting flat ripples" or "plain wavefronts." The speaker's tone is informative and slightly enthusiastic.

The clip starts with a male speaker discussing the shape of wavefronts. He explains that they're usually spherical for point sources and in 2D they would be circular.
He then continues, indicating sources far away result in flat wavefronts.
He mentions how wavefronts from the sun on the Earth are assumed to be plain wavefronts due to the great distance.
He reminds the listeners that there's no aether medium, and light is an electromagnetic wave.
He ends by pointing out why the speaker likes to start with Huygens's theory.
